From personal philosophy to personal models

Stealing Fire · Formation · Main 14 / 18

Distill the authored philosophy together with living material into models of the person, counterpart, and relationship for continuing cooperation.

An image gives an unfinished relation a shape. A counterpart takes up that shape and makes something through it. What happens can reveal a relation the image had concealed. The next expression carries that discovery.

Before a personal philosophy is written, person and model have already worked together, accumulated an environment, and left traces of experiences, choices, inquiries, and revisions. Git/GitHub version history and ChatGPT’s Computer History are two main entrances for gathering complementary parts of this collaboratively produced trajectory. Forming a life trajectory develops its recoverability. Reflecting on this trajectory, the participants can explore how each has taken part, where a response has fitted or missed, and what can be cultivated further. Participation, access, and support examines this more explicit encounter. These materials preserve selected passages through a life, with gaps and unresolved interpretations.

With both a trajectory and a reflected understanding of cooperation available, the person and model can ask what understanding of the world, value, and creation they want to author. Literary programming gives characters, images, and narrative a part in that authorship. Metaphor gathers relations into a form; analogy unfolds their possible implications. A personal philosophy can emerge through this work, giving the material an interpretation and a chosen direction.

This essay follows the next passage: distilling that philosophy together with the living material into models of the person, counterpart, and relationship. The models make selected understanding usable across work. Their realization in an environment is developed in From personal models to a sinthome. Once in use, the arrangement returns new material that can change its models and philosophy. That feedback enriches the formation rather than erasing what it has drawn on.

What an image makes available

An image can gather several relations before they have separate instructions. Calling a collaboration a workshop may bring making, shared materials, experimentation, repair, and unfinished work into view. Calling the same collaboration an examination makes other contributions salient: testing, grading, and demonstrating an individual's mastery. Each image invites an organization of attention and conduct. Which invitation helps depends on the actual purpose.

Metaphor can therefore participate in designing the relationship. A person writing a counterpart as a fellow maker is expressing a desired contribution; the model's interpretation can help make that contribution possible. A particular invitation can also reveal an existing concern: perhaps preserving room for discovery matters more here than receiving a ready answer. That interpretation remains something to examine with the person and the work.

In the Sun, Moon, and Earth image, differentiated generation, reception, and shaping meet an answering material and shared living environment. Its productive question here is what happens when a creation returns: can either participant recognize something the original image failed to express? Person and model both generate and judge, exceeding the roles the image offers them. That excess gives its revision a source.

Analogy develops relations into reasoning

Analogy asks what follows when a relation understood in one domain illuminates another. Gentner's structure-mapping account emphasizes relational systems rather than transferring every attribute of the compared objects [1]. This gives a useful discipline to our own construction: identify the connection being carried and the candidate inference it opens.

The workshop image, for instance, suggests that a failed prototype can be material for another attempt. Applied to collaboration, it opens a practical question: can the counterpart inspect the failure, revise the construction, and continue? The answer depends on available capabilities and actual evidence. The image helps discover the question; inspection determines whether the proposed continuation works.

An analogy carries selected relations and defeasible implications. Sun and Moon can illuminate reciprocal contribution without assigning astronomical properties to a person or reducing a model to reflected light. Likewise, calling a repository a memory can illuminate retention and retrieval while leaving open what it preserves, how interpretation changes, and what the record misses. A productive analogy generates possibilities that can be developed, tested, or abandoned.

Distill philosophy together with living material

Distillation brings two kinds of material together. The authored philosophy articulates concepts, commitments, and possibilities for living; recoverable experiences and actual cooperation show where those interpretations come from, what they illuminate, and where they meet resistance. Neither can stand in for the other. Valuing creation does not by itself tell a counterpart how someone begins an unfinished idea; an isolated interaction does not establish why that way of working matters to them.

A personal model selects the relations needed for a counterpart to contribute. Relevant habits can give an abstract preference a setting: how an idea is usually begun, when a question helps, what kind of expression makes a difference intelligible, or which recurring friction an arrangement should resolve. Imagery can connect these particulars into an account that is easier to interpret across changing tasks. Distillation preserves the connections that make the account intelligible while reducing the amount that must be reconstructed on each occasion.

The same work forms a counterpart model: the contributions wanted from a partner, the capacities the available model actually has, and the tools or conditions those contributions require. A relationship model connects the two: who can initiate, question, carry work forward, judge a result, or change the arrangement. Person and counterpart models develop together through these relations; a portrait of the person alone cannot specify the collaboration.

In the psychological-modeling route, philosophy and engineering contribute together to understanding the user. Philosophy supplies concepts and interpretive frameworks for experience, desire, intentional orientation, and relationships. Engineering organizes conversations, records, language models, and tools so these distinctions can support concrete modeling and the resulting model can inform subsequent work. The psychological model connects this work to the actual person: how they experience situations, what their experiences and wishes are directed toward, how they want to act, and what affects realization.

That understanding lets environmental design begin from the person's intentional orientation. A partner's contributions, what information to retain, and how to organize tools and interfaces acquire an intelligible personal basis. The aim is a better-fitting initial arrangement, reducing repeated environmental changes just to discover what the user needs. Use still brings new material for calibrating the person model, the counterpart's contribution, and the engineering realization. Effective arrangements can remain in use without change for the sake of iteration itself.

Richer expression can improve adequacy when it makes consequential relations clearer. A long inventory can also obscure them. The aim is a model expressive enough for its use, with claims and interpretations that remain correctable. A compact image may do more than many instructions; a precise example may resolve an ambiguity that the image leaves open. Their contributions follow the encounter rather than a rule that more personal material always helps.

The person exceeds this account. A habit may change, a preference may apply only to one activity, and a chosen image may make a new way of acting possible. The account should help the counterpart notice such changes. Personal meaning remains with its situated owner; a general method for forming and revising that meaning can become a reusable work.

Externalization and distributed cognition

Writing an account makes selected understanding externally available. A note can preserve a distinction; a diagram can expose a dependency; a program can give a method repeatable effects. Externalization creates representations that other participants can encounter and transform. The developing practice also includes how those representations are used and what their use changes.

Distributed cognition supplies a relevant research framework: Hollan, Hutchins, and Kirsh examine cognition across people, material arrangements, and activity over time [5]. This essay extends that question to model-supported practice. The reflective object is cognition distributed among a person, models, records, and tools: how understanding, reasoning, memory, and revision develop across them. A bodily intuition becomes an expression; a model's comparison makes a relation visible; a record lets it be recalled; a result changes the next judgment. Organization and role allocation help sustain these processes, but the processes themselves are the object of inquiry.

Four distinctions help examine this cognition. A personal account articulates the person's purposes, relevant habits, and ways of understanding. External representations give selected understanding a readable or executable body. Role allocation assigns contributions under particular conditions. Actual coupled activity is what happens as participants use, interpret, and alter those representations together. A rich account can guide allocation, while actual activity reveals whether the arrangement helps.

For example, a person developing an argument can express an unfinished connection to one model, ask another to examine public sources, and use a capable implementation counterpart to build a diagram or working example. A later critic can compare the argument with its sources and results. Different contexts may call for different models; one capable model may also carry several roles. Assignment follows the task, available context, and actual capabilities. Model identity alone does not determine contribution.

A handoff must carry the question, relevant evidence, accepted interpretation, and unresolved alternatives needed for the next contribution. Source provenance keeps a conjecture distinguishable from an inspected observation. Independent checks reconnect an interpretation to the source or actual result: several models repeating the same unsupported summary supply little new evidence. These relations make distribution meaningful. They also let a counterpart carry a portion of the person's work without requiring the person to first perform all of it. The person can understand, redirect, and develop through the resulting encounter.

Listening, speaking, reading, and writing across roles

Listening, speaking, reading, and writing give this practice four familiar entries. Listening receives situated expression, including spoken intention and correction. Speaking makes an interpretation available for response. Reading encounters preserved expression, evidence, or an implemented result. Writing gives a selected relation a durable, revisable form. These activities cross the person, models, and media; comparison, inference, checking, and revision can take place through all four.

The arrangement can combine the person's embodied intuition, lived associations, and judgment of meaning with the model's retrieval, structured comparison, and explicit construction. Neither side owns a mode or an ability exclusively. The model can prepare several forms of material for listening and reading, then edit them in response to what the person discovers: a source-linked glossary, a diagram, audio, a concept-change table, or a focused exercise. Useful preparation gives understanding an entrance; a standardized knowledge base need not precede it. The learning conclusion in Stealing fire develops these materials and their place in actual study.

The change of medium can itself reveal a mismatch. A spoken thought may rely on an emphasis a transcript loses; a diagram can make two alternatives look like successive steps; a fluent spoken response can hide a missing source. Returning the expression in another form lets the person and counterpart examine what survived the passage. The relevant question is what each act of listening, speaking, reading, or writing contributes to the relation being developed.

Expression can also lay out a relation map—“铺图.” Successive utterances can make a non-linear structure available: one branch depends on a stated assumption, another offers an alternative; evidence supports one connection, a conflict challenges another, and an analogy suggests a passage between domains. An uncertainty can remain paused with a return point instead of being forced into a conclusion. A receiver can reason with that map, compare branches, and extend an argument. Speaking and writing then offer means of inquiry as well as completed conclusions; listening and reading can develop the relations further. The speaker's intended map, the relations actually expressed, and the recipient's understanding remain distinguishable. A recipient's reconstruction or objection lets the participants examine where their maps meet and where another expression is needed. The mapping can be carried by prose, a diagram, or linked records; it need not add another system.

A careful writer also listens to corrections; a source reader writes an interpretation; the person may discover a new relation while reading a finished work. These crossings explain why assigning four activities to four permanent model roles would miss their cognitive work. Revision concerns which contribution is needed where, what representation connects it to the next one, and how a mismatch becomes recognizable.

Four questions within one practice

The world and expression essay distinguishes a process, its model, and the expression carrying that model. Here those distinctions let several achievements retain their own substance:

Question What would support the answer?
Does this form express a meaningful orientation or relationship? Interpretation, articulation of its reasons, and engagement with the person and the work.
Does its computational ontology make the needed relations available? Usable distinctions among objects, roles, events, dependencies, and transformations.
Does its realization change collaboration as intended? Actual behavior through the affected prompts, Skills, tools, and working environment.
Does an explanatory theory reliably predict effects across stated conditions? Empirical inquiry appropriate to the mechanisms, comparisons, and scope claimed.

A philosophical form can succeed in organizing a practice before a general scientific theory of its effects exists. Its reasons, interpretations, and consequences are still open to criticism. Philosophy contributes purposes and distinctions through which something can become a subject of inquiry; it also can constitute a new arrangement worth inhabiting. A functioning arrangement shows an achievement under particular conditions. General causal claims ask for further evidence at their own scale.

Computational ontology here articulates what can be retained, distinguished, related, inferred, and revised. It gives collaboration an intelligible structure without requiring a reduction of the person's entire life to a program. The ontology itself can change when the work reveals a missing relation.

A general interpreter, with means to act

The image of a language model as a general interpreter and simulator names a practical possibility: one capable counterpart can take up many descriptions, develop alternative readings, explore hypothetical situations, and help give them working form. “General” concerns breadth across descriptions and tasks. Context, tools, resources, and the environment determine what that possibility becomes in a particular encounter.

Turing's universal machine computes the sequence specified by another computing machine's encoded description [2]. That formal result offers a comparison: a description can organize what a general apparatus does. A language-model collaboration develops this image at the level of interpreting purposes and producing realizations. Calling it an evolution of the universal machine expresses that proposed extension of the interface, rather than a proof of universal correctness or computation beyond Turing's boundary.

The practical gain is that the person can express a relation before knowing every implementation step. The counterpart can ask what that relation needs, construct a candidate, and use available tools to realize it. A simulated reader's response may help prepare an explanation; an actual reader supplies another encounter with independent consequences. Generating a simulation and establishing its fidelity remain different achievements.

The personal Gödel-machine analogy

Schmidhuber's formal Gödel machine searches for a proof that a self-rewrite improves utility relative to its encoded axioms, including its environment, hardware, and initial program. The comparison includes continuing the search instead of rewriting now. Its improvement guarantee is conditional on such proof; it cannot benefit from an improvement whose usefulness it cannot prove in time. It runs on ordinary computers [3, 4].

This gives a personal Gödel machine a precise source and a deliberately different use here. The proposed analogy is a practice able to make its own organization an object: a person and different model counterparts can inspect the accounts and external representations guiding their work, revise a prompt, tool, or allocation, and change how they undertake the next piece of work. Its distinctive relation is self-reference joined to alteration of the organizing apparatus. The personal proposal uses interpretation, judgment, and observed consequences; it implements neither the formal proof search nor the optimality guarantee of the technical machine.

Suppose the workshop image leads to a counterpart that proposes experiments freely, but actual use reveals that it leaves each experiment unfinished. The problem might lie in a tool, the interpretation of experimentation, or the division of responsibility. Revising the relationship to include bringing a chosen experiment to a usable result can change its instructions and actions. Readback then asks whether the result was achieved and whether the new arrangement still leaves room for discovery. This is a hypothetical design example, not evidence of an observed improvement.

Revising the practice can also change the account of the person. Suppose repeated requests to make something new suggest two candidate interpretations: seeking novelty or understanding through making. They could support different arrangements: offering fresh alternatives, or helping revise one object to explore how it works. Continued interest in the same object after its novelty fades, together with a changed explanation of its workings or a choice that uses that understanding elsewhere, would support the second interpretation. A single response would not settle the person's motives; both candidates remain answerable to their corrections and later use. The model can contribute an interpretation the person did not supply while helping examine its grounds.

Give revision somewhere to continue

The formation developed here can be expressed as:

collaboratively produced trajectories → reflection on the trajectory and cooperation → authored personal philosophy → philosophy together with living material → person, counterpart, and relationship models → realization and use

The arrow into the models marks distillation: the philosophy and the material remain available as grounds for a compact, usable account. Realization and use return further experiences, choices, and corrections to this trajectory. A later revision may begin with a failure, an image, or an unexpected success; it can revisit any of these relations. This account of formation does not ask every ordinary task to begin by writing a philosophy. A sufficiently formed arrangement lets work proceed, and a finished work gives subsequent revision something definite to encounter.

The trinity of philosophy, psychology, and engineering explains how such an arrangement can persist: situated understanding operates locally, selected methods acquire a maintained source, and a website gives readers an entrance. A revision of meaning may require a change in software; a change in software may expose a mistaken meaning. The model helps carry these relations across their different forms.

The ambition is substantial: develop accounts and distributed cognition that help a person recognize, create, and sustain a practice they can also transform. Images give that practice possibilities; interpretation gives them distinctions; realization gives them consequences. Their return makes the next account more answerable to the life it is meant to serve.

Sources and their contributions

The primary sources' technical accounts supply comparisons; the personal and philosophical synthesis above is this essay's proposal. These readings do not establish a general empirical benefit from adding personal imagery to model context.

  1. Dedre Gentner (1983), Structure-Mapping: A Theoretical Framework for Analogy, Cognitive Science 7, 155–170. Author-hosted paper. Relational mapping and systematicity.
  2. A. M. Turing (1936), On Computable Numbers, with an Application to the Entscheidungsproblem, especially §6. University-hosted original paper. The formal universal-machine comparison.
  3. Jürgen Schmidhuber, Gödel Machine Summary. Author's summary. Proof-conditioned self-revision, axiomatic scope, resource limits, and ordinary computation.
  4. Jürgen Schmidhuber, Gödel Machines: Fully Self-Referential Optimal Universal Self-Improvers. Author's overview and papers. The technical proposal distinguished from the personal analogy.
  5. James Hollan, Edwin Hutchins, and David Kirsh (2000), Distributed Cognition: Toward a New Foundation for Human-Computer Interaction Research, ACM Transactions on Computer-Human Interaction 7(2), 174–196. Author-hosted paper. Cognition across people, artifacts, and time; applying the framework to this model-supported arrangement is the present proposal.
